A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
human lung fibroblast chondroitin sulfates are heterogeneous in terms of their core proteins and their mode of association with the cell surface.

the chondroitin 4-sulfate chains of human fibroblast membrane chondroitin sulfates are attached by an O-glycosidic linkage to the hydroxylysine residues of the 52-kDa core proteins and by an N-glycosidically linked oligosaccharide to the 90-kDa core proteins.

we identified a new type of membrane-associated chondrotin sulfate proteogylcans that are produced by human fibroblats and that are also found on stromal cells in the lung, on Kupffer cells and on epidermal cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the chondroitin sulfates that are found in human fibroblast cultures are a mixture of proteoglycan forms that have different biochemical, biological, and immunological properties and that may be involved in different biological functions.
the chondroitin sulfates of the small membrane-associated proteoglycants are exposed to the extracellular space and are probably important for cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions.

there is a family of chondroitin sulfates proteoglycants in the human lung that are membrane-bound and that are not identical to the previously characterized chondroitin proteoglycan core protein, aggrecan.
